**表面加工质量的检验** Surface quality inspection turns very small variations in a surface into visible changes in fringes.
The source gives a testing precision of $\frac{1}{10}$ of a wavelength, approximately $10^{-6}$ centimetres.

Place the surface being tested close to a very smooth reference plane, leaving a thin, wedge-shaped air layer between them, as in Figure 201.
Light reflected from the surfaces on either side of this air layer comes from the same incident beam and overlaps to form interference fringes.

With flat surfaces, the air-layer thickness changes regularly along the wedge, producing regularly arranged fringes.
A bump or hollow changes the local layer thickness and the path difference of the reflected light, bending the fringes.
The source states that surface variations of $10^{-6}$ centimetres already cause noticeable bending.

Coherent light waves have the same frequency and a stable phase difference, so the timing of their vibrations relative to each other does not change unpredictably.
Splitting the same beam along different paths and then bringing the parts together can preserve this relationship.

An instrument that uses interference for measurement is called an interferometer.
A change in optical path shifts the bright and dark fringes, allowing precise measurements of quantities such as the wavelength of light or the refractive index of a gas, as well as specialized tests.

**光学增透** Antireflection treatment addresses reflection at optical-glass surfaces.
Camera lenses, projector lenses, periscopes, and similar instruments contain lenses and prisms, so light encounters many surfaces in succession.

The source describes camera lenses with more than $10$ reflecting surfaces and submarine periscopes with as many as $40$.
At normal incidence, each surface can reflect $5$ to $9\%$ of the incident energy, and repeated reflections reduce the light travelling forward.

In the instruments described by the source, only $10$ to $20\%$ of the incident energy sometimes passes through, leaving the image dim.
Reflection can also reduce image clarity.
Some light reflects repeatedly inside the instrument before emerging forwards, but no longer converges at the correct image position, becoming stray light that produces a veiling haze.

Reducing surface reflection allows more light to form a bright image and reduces interference from stray reflections.
This treatment is called antireflection treatment, or optical transmission enhancement.
It does not amplify light: it reduces the light that would otherwise be reflected back.
